title: Unit 1: Python Language Fundamentals, Datatypes & Immutability
content:
Python is a general-purpose, high-level, interpreted programming language developed by Guido Van Rossum in 1989 and officially released on February 20, 1991. The name was inspired by the BBC comedy show 'Monty Python's Flying Circus'.

11 Key Features of Python:
1. Simple and easy to learn (only 33 reserved keywords, English-like syntax).
2. Freeware and Open Source (maintained by Python Software Foundation - PSF).
3. High-level programming language (programmer-friendly, automatic memory management and garbage collection).
4. Platform Independent (Write Once, Run Anywhere via Python Virtual Machine - PVM for Windows, Linux, Mac).
5. Portability (applications migrate across platforms without code modifications).
6. Dynamically Typed (types allocated automatically at runtime based on assigned value, no explicit declaration).
7. Both Procedure Oriented (like C) and Object Oriented (like C++, Java).
8. Interpreted (executed line by line by PVM, no separate manual compilation step).
9. Extensible (can integrate legacy C, C++, and Java code for high performance).
10. Embedded (Python scripts can be embedded within C/C++ applications).
11. Extensive Standard Library (huge collection of built-in modules: math, random, os, sys, re, etc.).

Flavours of Python:
- CPython: Standard implementation written in C.
- Jython (JPython): Runs on Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
- IronPython: Built for C#.NET platform.
- PyPy: Features a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler inside PVM for significantly higher execution speed.
- RubyPython: For Ruby platforms.
- AnacondaPython: Specially customized for large-scale data processing and data science.

Identifier Rules:
- Allowed characters: alphabet symbols (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9), and underscore (_).
- Identifiers cannot start with a digit (e.g. 123total is invalid, total123 is valid).
- Identifiers are case-sensitive (total vs TOTAL).
- Cannot use any of the 33 reserved keywords as identifiers.
- Note on Keywords: Out of 33 keywords, only 3 start with an uppercase letter: True, False, None. All other 30 keywords are lowercase.

14 Built-in Data Types:
int, float, complex, bool, str, bytes, bytearray, range, list, tuple, set, frozenset, dict, None.

Fundamental Types & Immutability:
- Fundamental types: int, float, complex, bool, str.
- In Python, everything is an Object. When an object is created, PVM reuses existing objects for small integers (-5 to 256) and strings via object interning to optimize memory and speed.
- Fundamental types are Immutable: Once created, their content cannot be changed in-place. Modifying a variable creates a new object in memory (`id(x)` changes).
- `is` vs `==`: `==` compares content/values, while `is` compares memory addresses (reference equality).

Base Conversions:
- Decimal (base 10, default), Binary (`0b` or `0B`), Octal (`0o` or `0O`), Hexadecimal (`0x` or `0X`).
- Conversion functions: `bin(x)`, `oct(x)`, `hex(x)`.
analogy: Think of variables in Python as sticky name tags attached to objects in a room. Multiple tags can point to the exact same object. When you 'change' an immutable number, you aren't repainting the number; you are simply peeling your sticky tag off and sticking it onto a brand-new number!
simplification_tips: Remember the 3 Capitalized Keywords: True, False, and None. All other 30 keywords in Python are entirely lowercase. Never declare variable types explicitly in Python; the PVM figures it out dynamically.
